body.text: American strength, rather than institutional consensus, would be the principal guarantor of peace

President Donald Trump’s address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly offered a striking articulation of the foreign-policy logic underpinning his second term. Over roughly 37 minutes, Trump sought to present an America that was not merely “back” but determined to shape the international order on its own terms. The central message was familiar: American strength, rather than institutional consensus, would be the principal guarantor of peace. “Peace through strength” was less a slogan than a framework for understanding Washington’s approach to a world that Trump portrayed as increasingly defined by threats, weak institutions and strategic competition.

Iran occupied the centre of this worldview. Trump described Tehran as the world’s leading sponsor of terrorism and reiterated that the United States would not permit Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon. His defence of US-Israeli military action was framed around preventing an Iranian nuclear breakthrough, while his rhetoric deliberately kept open the possibility of both diplomacy and escalation. Iran, in this formulation, faces a stark choice: negotiate on terms acceptable to Washington or confront the possibility of overwhelming force. The call for comprehensive economic isolation until Tehran abandons its nuclear ambitions, support for terrorism and attacks on shipping reflected a broader Trumpian preference for coercive leverage over prolonged multilateral diplomacy. Significantly, this rhetoric coexisted with contacts between American and Iranian officials on the margins of the UN meeting, underscoring the transactional character of Trump’s diplomacy.

The Western Hemisphere was presented in equally stark terms. Trump’s references to Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, oil resources and the doctrine that “to the victor belong the spoils” suggested that Washington increasingly sees the hemisphere as an area in which American primacy should be both asserted and enforced. Venezuela was linked to a larger argument about energy, strategic autonomy and the refusal to permit hostile powers to establish a foothold close to the United States. Cartels were elevated to the category of foreign terrorist organisations and compared with ISIS, while military action against maritime drug trafficking was cited as evidence of a more muscular approach. Cuba, meanwhile, was portrayed as a failed communist state whose political future was effectively predetermined. Mexico also appeared within this wider security framework.

Trump’s claims regarding conflict resolution served another important purpose. He sought to establish himself not simply as a disruptor of the international system but as a deal-maker capable of delivering results where conventional diplomacy had failed. Cambodia-Thailand, Kosovo-Serbia, Rwanda-DRC, India-Pakistan, Armenia-Azerbaijan and Gaza were presented as examples of conflicts that his administration had settled or helped bring to an end. The underlying method, however, was distinctly Trumpian: personal relationships, economic leverage, tariffs and American power were treated as more consequential than institutional processes. Ukraine was similarly framed as a problem that Washington was actively managing with both sides, with Trump suggesting that an agreement could emerge sooner than many expect.

The Arctic and Greenland represented perhaps the clearest expression of the geopolitical logic behind this approach. Trump’s emphasis on an expanded American military presence and new security arrangements involving Denmark and Greenland reflected the growing strategic importance of the Arctic. For Washington, the region is no longer a peripheral frontier. It is increasingly connected to great-power competition, maritime access, critical infrastructure and the defence of North America. The insistence that adversarial military activity or sensitive investments cannot be permitted without American approval points to an emerging conception of the Arctic as a theatre in which strategic denial will be as important as conventional deterrence.

The speech was also a frontal challenge to the assumptions of the post-Cold War international order. Trump portrayed the UN as an institution captured by what he described as a “far-left agenda” and criticised globalist bureaucracies, international taxation and attempts to impose common regulatory frameworks. His opposition to a global carbon tax and his rejection of international constraints on artificial intelligence reflected a consistent proposition: Washington should retain maximum freedom of action in areas it considers central to national power.

AI was particularly revealing. Trump’s embrace of American leadership in what he called “super intelligence” was accompanied by scepticism toward international safety regimes. The message was that technological supremacy should be accelerated rather than constrained by global regulatory structures. In this sense, technology policy fits comfortably within the broader foreign-policy architecture of the speech: strategic advantage is to be cultivated domestically, while international institutions are prevented from limiting the exercise of American power.
The preference is consequently for bilateral bargains, transactional relationships and demonstrable leverage.

Trump’s attacks on the Human Rights Council and the International Criminal Court further demonstrated the depth of his resistance to supranational constraints. Sovereignty remained the organising principle, whether the issue was immigration, borders, cultural policy, taxation or technological regulation. The UN, in this conception, has value when it advances American interests but becomes problematic when it attempts to constrain the United States.

There is therefore a larger strategic story beneath the rhetoric. Trump’s second-term foreign policy is increasingly defined by the conviction that American primacy is best preserved not through the expansion of multilateral institutions but through the direct application of economic, military and technological power. Alliances and institutions have not disappeared from this worldview, but they occupy a different place. They are instruments rather than ends in themselves.

This represents a significant departure from the liberal internationalist assumption that American leadership is most effective when embedded within rules and institutions. Trump instead appears to believe that American power is weakened when those rules constrain Washington’s freedom of action. The preference is consequently for bilateral bargains, transactional relationships and demonstrable leverage. The willingness to threaten maximum force while simultaneously leaving room for negotiation is not necessarily contradictory; it is central to the strategy.

Yet the speech also revealed the limits of such an approach. Several of Trump’s claims regarding oil resources, conflict resolution and the scale of cartel interdiction have been questionable, to say the least. The distinction between declaring a conflict “ended” and producing a durable political settlement is particularly important. Likewise, claims about energy dominance need to be assessed against actual global reserves and production rather than political rhetoric.

Trump presented an America confident in its military and economic weight, sceptical of international institutions, unwilling to accept external constraints and increasingly prepared to define regional spheres of strategic interest.

The larger significance of the address, therefore, lies less in any individual assertion than in the worldview it assembled. Trump presented an America confident in its military and economic weight, sceptical of international institutions, unwilling to accept external constraints and increasingly prepared to define regional spheres of strategic interest. The language was unmistakably about primacy.

For the international system, this carries considerable implications. A United States that sees sovereignty and leverage as the principal currencies of international politics will inevitably place greater pressure on allies, institutions and adversaries alike. The question is not whether America remains powerful. It plainly does. The more consequential question is how that power will be converted into a sustainable international order.

Trump’s answer at the UN was clear: through strength, bargaining power and the willingness to act unilaterally when necessary. Whether that produces a more stable international system will depend not only on American capabilities, but also on how other major powers respond to an increasingly transactional conception of global order.
